lead: A signal on an interval behaves like a vector with one component for every instant. Vector algebra then carries over. The inner product measures how much of one signal lies along another, the norm is the size of a signal (the square root of its energy), and two signals are orthogonal when their inner product is zero. The best approximation of one signal by a multiple of another is the projection you already use for vectors. The Fourier series and digital modems rest on this picture.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for signal notation and Chapter 1.2 for the energy of a signal.

blocks.text: Take two vectors A and B. The component of A along B is cB, with c = A·B / |B|². What is left, the error vector e = A − cB, is perpendicular to B, and this c makes |e| as small as possible: any other multiple of B leaves a longer error.
A signal on an interval a ≤ t ≤ b has one component for every instant. Replace the sum Σ AₖBₖ of the dot product by an integral and you have the inner product of two signals.

blocks.where: a and b are the interval limits in seconds; y*(t) is the complex conjugate of y(t), and for real signals y*(t) = y(t). In discrete time the integral becomes Σ x[n] y*[n] over the chosen samples.
‖x‖ is the norm of x. ‖x‖² is the energy of x on [a, b] (Chapter 1.2), so the norm is the square root of the energy.

blocks.text: The inner product is one number. A large positive value means the two signals rise and fall together on the interval; a large negative value means one is close to a negative copy of the other; zero means neither has any component along the other. For complex signals judge the size |⟨x, y⟩|.

Approximate a real signal f₁(t) by c f₂(t) over t₁ < t < t₂. The error signal is fₑ(t) = f₁(t) − c f₂(t). Choose c to make the mean square error ε = (1/(t₂ − t₁)) ∫ fₑ²(t) dt as small as possible, by setting dε/dc = 0.

dε/dc = (1/(t₂ − t₁)) ∫ 2[f₁(t) − c f₂(t)][−f₂(t)] dt = 0
⇒  ∫ f₁(t) f₂(t) dt = c ∫ f₂²(t) dt
⇒  c₁₂ = ∫ f₁(t) f₂(t) dt / ∫ f₂²(t) dt = ⟨f₁, f₂⟩ / ‖f₂‖²
blocks.where: every integral runs from t₁ to t₂; c₁₂ is the component of f₁ along f₂, the same formula as c = A·B / |B|² for vectors.

blocks.text: With this c₁₂ the error energy is ‖f₁‖² − c₁₂²‖f₂‖²: the energy of f₁ minus the energy of the part that was kept. The first line above also says ∫ fₑ(t) f₂(t) dt = 0: the error left over is orthogonal to f₂, exactly like the perpendicular error vector.

If ⟨f₁, f₂⟩ = 0 then c₁₂ = 0. The signal f₂ cannot help to approximate f₁ at all, and the two are called orthogonal on that interval. Some syllabi call this topic the analogy between vectors and signals.

sections.h3: Orthogonal sets and the coefficient formula

blocks.text: A set of nonzero signals φ₁, φ₂, … is orthogonal on an interval when ⟨φₘ, φₙ⟩ = 0 for every m ≠ n. Write Kₙ = ‖φₙ‖² for the energy of φₙ; it is never zero, because the zero signal is not allowed in the set. The set is orthonormal when every Kₙ = 1.
Orthogonality makes the coefficients independent of each other. Write x ≈ Σ cₙφₙ and take the inner product of both sides with φₘ. Every term with n ≠ m gives zero, so a single term survives:
cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩ / Kₙ = (1/Kₙ) ∫ₐᵇ x(t) φₙ*(t) dt
blocks.where: cₙ is the coefficient of φₙ; Kₙ = ∫ₐᵇ |φₙ(t)|² dt is the energy of φₙ on [a, b]; for an orthonormal set cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩.

items: Fix the interval; orthogonality means nothing without it.
Check that the set is orthogonal on that interval.
Divide to get cₙ. The sum Σ cₙφₙ is the best approximation of x that the set can give.

blocks.text: Whether the best approximation equals x, leaving no error energy, depends on whether the set is complete. Chapter 1.8 answers that and adds up the energy with Parseval's relation.

figure.caption: The square wave f(t) and its best single-term approximation c₁₂ sin t with c₁₂ = 4/π ≈ 1.27. The shaded gap is the error signal; its energy, about 1.19 of the total 2π, is the smallest any multiple of sin t can leave.

spec.aria: A square wave equal to +1 from 0 to π and −1 from π to 2π, with the sine curve 1.27 sin t drawn over it and the gaps between them shaded.

examples.question: A square wave is f(t) = 1 for 0 < t < π and f(t) = −1 for π < t < 2π. Approximate it over (0, 2π) by c sin t. (a) Find the best value of c. (b) Find the error energy and the mean square error. (c) What fraction of the energy of f does the approximation carry?
steps: Here f₁ = f and f₂ = sin t on t₁ = 0, t₂ = 2π, so c₁₂ = ∫ f(t) sin t dt / ∫ sin² t dt, both integrals over (0, 2π).
Numerator: over (0, π), ∫ sin t dt = [−cos t] = −cos π + cos 0 = 2. Over (π, 2π), ∫ (−1) sin t dt = [cos t] = cos 2π − cos π = 2. Total 4.
Denominator: ∫ sin² t dt = ∫ (1 − cos 2t)/2 dt = 2π/2 = π, because cos 2t integrates to zero over two whole periods.
(a) c₁₂ = 4/π ≈ 1.273, so f(t) ≈ (4/π) sin t ≈ 1.273 sin t.
(b) The energy of f is ‖f‖² = ∫ 1 dt = 2π ≈ 6.283, since f² = 1 everywhere. The part kept has energy c₁₂²‖sin t‖² = (16/π²)(π) = 16/π ≈ 5.093.
Error energy = 2π − 16/π ≈ 6.283 − 5.093 = 1.190. Mean square error ε = 1.190/(2π) = 1 − 8/π² ≈ 0.189.
(c) Fraction kept = (16/π)/(2π) = 8/π² ≈ 0.811, so one sine carries about 81 % of the energy.
Check the minimum with another value, c = 1: error energy = ∫ (f − sin t)² dt = 2π − 2(1)(4) + (1)²π = 3π − 8 ≈ 1.425, larger than 1.190.
examples.answer: c₁₂ = 4/π ≈ 1.273; error energy 2π − 16/π ≈ 1.190 and mean square error 1 − 8/π² ≈ 0.189; the single sine carries 8/π² ≈ 81 % of the energy.

examples.question: On 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 take φ₁(t) = 1 and φ₂(t) = 2t − 1. (a) Show that they are orthogonal. (b) Find K₁ and K₂. (c) Expand x(t) = t in this set.
steps: (a) ⟨φ₁, φ₂⟩ = ∫₀¹ (2t − 1) dt = [t² − t] from 0 to 1 = 0 − 0 = 0. Both signals are nonzero, so they are orthogonal on [0, 1].
Rebuild: c₁φ₁ + c₂φ₂ = 1/2 + (1/2)(2t − 1) = t. Two terms reproduce x exactly, so no error energy is left.

traps: Orthogonality depends on the interval. φ₁ = 1 and φ₂ = 2t − 1 have inner product 0 on [0, 1], but ∫₀² (2t − 1) dt = 4 − 2 = 2 on [0, 2].
Divide by Kₙ = ‖φₙ‖², not by ‖φₙ‖. In worked example 2, dividing ⟨t, φ₂⟩ = 1/6 by ‖φ₂‖ = 0.577 gives 0.289 instead of the correct c₂ = 0.5.
For complex signals conjugate the second signal. Without the star, the inner product of e<sup>jt</sup> with itself over (0, 2π) comes out 0 instead of its energy 2π.
The best sine for the square wave is 1.273 sin t, not 1·sin t: it must be taller than the square wave to make up for being too low near t = 0 and t = π.

quiz.q: Define the inner product and the norm of two real signals on [a, b].
quiz.a: ⟨x, y⟩ = ∫ₐᵇ x(t)y(t) dt. ‖x‖ = √⟨x, x⟩, the square root of the energy of x on [a, b].

quiz.q: When are two signals orthogonal on an interval?
quiz.a: When both are nonzero and ⟨x, y⟩ = ∫ₐᵇ x(t)y*(t) dt = 0 on that interval.

quiz.q: Why is the error left by the best approximation c₁₂f₂(t) orthogonal to f₂?
quiz.a: Setting dε/dc = 0 gives ∫ (f₁ − c₁₂f₂) f₂ dt = 0, which says ⟨fₑ, f₂⟩ = 0. If part of the error still lay along f₂, a different c would remove it and lower the error, so at the minimum none is left, just as with a perpendicular error vector.

quiz.q: On 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 approximate f₁(t) = t by a constant c·1. Find c₁₂ and the error energy.
quiz.a: c₁₂ = ∫₀¹ t dt / ∫₀¹ 1 dt = 1/2. Error energy = ‖t‖² − c₁₂²(1) = 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12 ≈ 0.083.

quiz.q: On (0, 2π) approximate the square wave of worked example 1 by c sin 3t. Find the best c.
quiz.a: Over (0, π), ∫ sin 3t dt = [−cos 3t/3] = 2/3; over (π, 2π), ∫ (−1) sin 3t dt = 2/3. Numerator 4/3. ∫ sin² 3t dt = π. c = 4/(3π) ≈ 0.424.

quiz.q: A student uses c₁ = ⟨x, φ₁⟩/K₁ with φ₁ = 1 and φ₂ = 2t − 1 on [0, 2], treating them as orthogonal. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: On [0, 2], ⟨φ₁, φ₂⟩ = 2, not 0. For x = c₁φ₁ + c₂φ₂, ⟨x, φ₁⟩ = c₁K₁ + 2c₂, so the cross term 2c₂ spoils c₁. The coefficient formula holds only for a set that is orthogonal on the interval used.

beyond: Not for the exam. OFDM modems make their subcarriers orthogonal over one symbol, so the receiver recovers each subcarrier's data with one inner product, and QAM places symbols in a two-dimensional signal space built from the cosine and sine of the carrier. Search "signal space representation" and "Gram–Schmidt for signals" to continue.
